title: Soil conservation

definition.text: Preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion, and the loss of fertility through overuse, acidification, salinization or chemical contamination.

facts.text: Its techniques include crop rotation, cover crops, conservation tillage and planted windbreaks, which affect both erosion and fertility.
Deforestation typically brings large-scale erosion, loss of soil nutrients and sometimes total desertification.
Farmers have practised soil conservation for millennia; the ancient Phoenicians ploughed on the contour on slopes of two to ten percent.
Government involvement in land management and soil conservation expanded greatly after the Dust Bowl, beginning in Franklin D. Roosevelt's first 100 days in 1933.
In Europe, the Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, winter cover crops, plant residues and grass margins for soil conservation.
Salinity, left when irrigation water evaporates or rises from shallow saline water tables, is estimated to affect about one third of the earth's arable land.
Each one percent increase in soil organic matter helps soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre.
Solving erosion also needs political and economic action, since how land is valued is a governance hurdle that cultural change can shift.

notes: The page's Salinity management, Soil organisms and Mineralization sections belong with Soil salinity control, Earthworm and Agrominerals (other chapters); its Contour ploughing, Terrace farming and Keyline design sections are folded into those entries. Perimeter runoff control matches Buffer strip and Grassed waterway (erosion chapter).

title: Soil-conservation farming

definition.text: Farming that combines no-till, green manures and other soil-enhancing practices to protect and rebuild the soil.

facts.text: Its advocates say it can revive damaged soil, minimize erosion, remove the need for nitrogen fertilizer or fungicide and protect crops in drought or flood, at lower labour and cost.
No-till and cover crops act as sinks for nitrogen and other nutrients, which raises soil organic matter.
Repeated ploughing degrades soil and kills its beneficial fungi and earthworms, and damaged soil may need several seasons to recover.
Critics call no-till and related methods impractical and costly, cite advantages of conventional tillage in some settings, and say no-till complicates pest control and residue management.

contested_note: Critics dispute that no-till and related conservation farming methods are practical and affordable for many growers.
notes: S:7b943f37a79e (mimicking 'the biology of barren lands') is unclear and was not used.

title: Windbreak

definition.text: One or more rows of trees or shrubs, also called a shelterbelt, planted to shelter land from the wind and protect soil from erosion.

facts.text: Shelterbelts are rows of trees set perpendicular to the prevailing wind, while woodlots are more extensive areas of woodland.
Evergreens protect all year, but deciduous trees may be enough if they are in leaf while the soil is bare.
Besides sharply reducing wind erosion, windbreaks improve the microclimate for crops, shelter beneficial birds, sequester carbon and improve the landscape.
They reduce evapotranspiration as well as erosion, and with woodlots they are used to fix the soil against desertification.
Farmers plant them to cut wind erosion of loess, and very light soils need them in dry weather.
Windbreaks also separate fields and protect them from pesticide spray drift.
Behind a windbreak the wind is slowest at about 3 to 5 times its height downwind, then recovers.
Farmers also use windbreaks to hold snow on fields, where it supplies water when it melts in spring.

notes: Re-anchored from Soil conservation#Windbreaks to the Windbreak article in the gap-fill pass.

title: Reducing pesticide use
article: Soil conservation#Reducing the use of pesticides

definition.text: Cutting pesticide use to protect soil, since pesticides can contaminate soil, nearby vegetation and water for a long time.

facts.text: Pesticides affect soil structure and its biotic and abiotic composition.

Alternatives include irradiation, cultivation methods, biological controls such as pheromones and microbial pesticides, genetic engineering and disrupting insect breeding; composted yard waste has also controlled pests.
Differentiated taxation schemes are among the options studied for reducing pesticide use.

definition.text: Applying operations, practices and treatments to protect soil and improve its performance, such as its fertility or mechanical behaviour.

facts.text: It takes in soil conservation, soil amendment and optimal soil health, and both conventional and organic farms need it to stay productive over decades.
Organic farming relies on soil health for almost all of its fertility and pest control, so it stresses soil management.
Controlling traffic on the soil surface reduces compaction, which can cut aeration and water infiltration.
Cover crops keep soil anchored and covered off-season, and rotations alternate high- and low-residue crops to keep plant material on the surface against erosion.
Conventional tillage disturbs soil most deeply; reduced-tillage and no-till keep residues on the surface for erosion protection and water retention.
Fertilizers add nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and potassium but often acidify soils, potassium fertilizer excepted.
Adding organic matter to the surface can raise soil carbon and the abundance and diversity of soil microbes.
Project Drawdown names improved nutrient management, conservation agriculture and regenerative agriculture as soil management steps for climate change mitigation.

title: Soil management and greenhouse gases

definition.text: The effect of how soils are managed on greenhouse gases: management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon, or store carbon dioxide as soil organic carbon.

facts.text: Fertilizer use, irrigation and tillage contribute to nitrous oxide emissions, and soil management accounts for over half of the agriculture sector's emissions.
Using biochar may cut nitrous oxide emissions from soils by an average of 54%.
Converting natural land to farmland releases carbon, and how much carbon a soil can store depends on climate, land-use history and management.
Cropland could sequester 0.5–1.2 Pg C/year and grazing and pasture land 0.3–0.7 Pg C/year.
Sequestration rises with more biomass inputs, smaller losses of soil organic carbon and a longer mean residence time of that carbon.
No-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation significantly enhance soil carbon sequestration and are more common in organic than conventional farming.

notes: S:dbf8f8685be7 (only 5% of US farmland under no-till and residue mulching) cites 2004 and is far below No-till farming's 21% for 2017; left out as dated.

title: Conservation agriculture

definition.text: A farming system, as defined by the FAO, that prevents loss of arable land and regenerates degraded land through minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and diverse plant species.

facts.text: Soil cover comes from mulch or cover crops, and disturbance is minimized by eliminating or greatly reducing ploughing, as in no-till farming.
By cutting ploughing it encourages earthworms and the formation of a mull-like agricultural humus form called agri-mull.
Mineral fertilizer use is reduced to the strict requirements of the crop and is sometimes unnecessary.
With regenerative and organic agriculture it is grouped as sustainable agriculture, an alternative to industrialized conventional farming.
Tillage, once thought to raise fertility through mineralization, is now seen to destroy organic matter and cause erosion and crusting.
The mulch layer slows runoff and softens raindrop impact, and keeps soil moisture and temperature higher than yearly tillage.
Producers can save 30% to 40% of time and labour with no-till.
Benefits can take many years, new planters or drills cost money, and in developing countries the residues it needs are traditionally fed to livestock.

notes: Re-anchored on the Conservation agriculture article in the gap-fill pass.

title: Cover crop

definition.text: A crop planted to cover the soil rather than to be harvested.

facts.text: Cover crops help manage erosion, fertility, soil quality, water, weeds, pests, diseases, biodiversity and wildlife in an agroecosystem.
They are often sown off-season after the cash crop is harvested and grown over winter, and they act as nurse crops that help the main crop survive.
Often grown solely against erosion, they protect the surface, scatter raindrop energy, slow overland flow and raise infiltration, while their roots anchor soil and add porosity.
They increase microbial activity, which improves nitrogen availability, nitrogen uptake by the following crop and yields.
A meta-analysis of 102 field studies found saturated hydraulic conductivity up about 106% and topsoil organic carbon and nitrogen up about 10% and 20%.
Microbial biomass carbon rose about 20% and particulate organic carbon nearly 50% compared with bare or fallow ground.
Trade-offs exist: cover crops may reduce water for the next crop or leave yields unchanged, especially in semi-arid regions or with poorly timed termination.
They are killed before the cash crop by mowing, tilling, discing, rolling or herbicide.

distinct_from: Cover crops in pest and disease control
notes: S:598272381043 is flagged CONTESTED but describes context-dependent and uncertain effects, not a dispute between sources; not marked contested.

title: Cover crops for soil fertility

definition.text: Growing cover crops, often legumes, to raise soil fertility, chiefly by supplying or conserving nitrogen.

facts.text: Fertility-building cover crops are called green manures; they are often ploughed under before maturity.
Leguminous cover crops, nodulated by bacteria such as Bradyrhizobium that fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium, can often supply all the nitrogen a crop needs.
This ability to stand in for chemical nitrogen fertilizer is called fertilizer replacement value.
Some scientists see biological nitrogen fixation, mainly through cover crops, as the only alternative to fossil-fuel-dependent industrial nitrogen fixation for future food production.
Nitrogen fertilizer lost to waterways causes eutrophication, as in the Gulf of Mexico's summer dead zone of over 22,000 square kilometres.
In Nigeria the velvet bean cover crop increased soil phosphorus availability after rock phosphate was applied.

distinct_from: Cover crops in pest and disease control

definition.text: A fast-growing crop, a type of cover crop, grown between two successive main crops.

facts.text: It takes up surplus nitrogen left from the previous crop, keeping it from loss by leaching, denitrification or volatilization; catch crops are usually fast-growing cereals.
The nitrogen it holds returns to the soil when it is worked in as green manure or decomposes.
Its residue roughens the surface against splash and runoff, and decaying roots leave biopores that increase infiltration.
Sowing date, harvest date and tillage decide its benefit; sowing later than recommended reduces its nitrogen uptake.

title: Cover crops and soil water

definition.text: The ways cover crops change how water enters, moves through and leaves a field's soil.

facts.text: By curbing erosion they reduce the rate and amount of water draining off fields, a risk to waterways downstream.
Their biomass shields the surface from rain, and their roots open pores that let water filter down instead of running off.
Greater infiltration can improve soil water storage and aquifer recharge.
Where water is scarce, cover crops used as mulch shade and cool the surface, reducing evaporation.

distinct_from: Cover crops in pest and disease control

title: Weed suppression by cover crops

definition.text: The control of weeds by cover crops, through competition while they grow and smothering or chemical inhibition after they die.

facts.text: A cover crop flattened on the surface forms a nearly impenetrable mat that blocks light, cutting weed germination; this is the smother effect.
Some cover crops release compounds that inhibit other plants, called allelopathy; examples include rye, hairy vetch, red clover, sorghum-sudangrass and mustards.
After termination, yellow sweetclover residues held weeds 75–97% below levels in fallow systems.
Rye cover crop residues used as mulch gave 80% to 95% control of early-season broadleaf weeds.

distinct_from: Cover crops in pest and disease control

title: Cover crops in pest and disease control

definition.text: Using cover crops to break pest and disease cycles, lure pests away as trap crops and attract their natural enemies.

facts.text: Mustards and other Brassicaceae suppress fungal diseases with toxic chemicals released as their glucosinolates break down.
Nematode-resistant white mustard and radish trap nematodes that enter their roots but cannot reproduce there, cutting populations by 70–99%.
Grasses, legumes and brassicas also raise soil organic matter and microbial activity, making cash crops more resilient to insect pests and pathogens.
Findings on cover crops and predator–pest dynamics are mixed, so effects depend on the cover crop type and management.

definition.text: Farming a field divided into long, narrow strips that alternate in a crop rotation, also called strip cropping.

facts.text: It is used where a slope is too steep, or no other method can prevent soil erosion.
Strips of close-sown hay, wheat or forage, serving mainly as cover crops, alternate with strips of row crops such as corn, soybeans, cotton or sugar beets.
Laid out along the approximate contour, the sod strips act as natural dams that slow water and hold back soil from the cultivated strips.
Strip width depends chiefly on average wind speed and slope gradient; strips are usually 25 feet (7.6 m) to 75 feet (23 m) wide, and 50 feet (15 m) suits most machinery.
In dry farming on the Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, fallow and cropped strips run at right angles to the prevailing wind to limit wind erosion of bare fields.
Contour strip cropping, used mainly on gentle slopes, makes the protective strips wider than the row-crop strips so they intercept runoff.
In strip intercropping the strips are narrower and contiguous, which suits machinery and lets neighbouring crops benefit from each other.
In the Midwestern United States, prairie strips of native plants serve as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters that build soil health and curb erosion.

title: Terrace (earthworks)

definition.text: A flat surface cut into a hill or mountainside for growing crops, usually built as a series of steps like a staircase.

facts.text: Terraced fields reduce both erosion and surface runoff and can hold irrigated crops such as rice.
Each terrace is itself protected from erosion by other soil barriers, and terracing is more common on small farms.
Terraced paddies are used for rice, wheat and barley across much of Asia, the Mediterranean Basin, Africa and South America.
Terraces in the Yemen Highlands date from the start of the Bronze Age in the 3rd millennium BC, and Levant terrace farming from as early as the 4th millennium BCE.
Andean terraces, or andenes, were developed by the Wari and others before 1000 AD to use shallow soil efficiently and irrigate crops, and were later adopted by the Inca.
Luminescence dating shows a major burst of Mediterranean terrace building in the later Middle Ages, around AD 1100–1600.
Long-term soil moisture management by terracing or irrigation can create anthraquic Anthrosols.
Scholars lack consensus on when the ancient terraces of the Jerusalem Mountains were built, with proposals ranging from the Bronze Age to the Roman and Byzantine periods.

contested_note: Scholars disagree on the construction dates of the Jerusalem Mountains terraces, and luminescence dates may reflect later modification.
notes: Folds in Soil conservation#Terrace farming (S:fa670b440b81, S:4e6f5d182b15, S:8b3bac187ece).

title: Terracette

definition.text: A landform of roughly parallel, step-like ridges on a steep hillside.

facts.text: These small, irregular steps are common on steep pastures, where soil creep or surface erosion is worsened by trampling sheep or cattle; they are also called catsteps or cattle terracing.
One explanation is that saturated soil swells and then shrinks as it dries, so particles creep slowly downhill; freeze–thaw and heating–cooling cycles can do the same.

Darwin (1904) thought grazing animals made them, but some end abruptly at rock faces or soil changes, livestock trails cut across others, and geomorphologists doubt animals alone could form such regular steps.

contested_note: Sources dispute whether grazing animals or soil processes such as creep and solifluction mainly form terracettes.
notes: Lead sentences S:105fee162abf and S:408ef7d643f3 carry BETTER SOURCE NEEDED tags; not used.

definition.text: Digging continuous trenches along the contour of a slope to conserve water and soil and raise crop yields, an easily applied technique in arid sub-Saharan areas.

facts.text: The trench catches water flowing downhill so it soaks into the soil, and crops between trenches draw on this subsoil reserve during the drier growing season.
Rainwater no longer runs straight off the hill, crops suffer less from later water shortage, and fertile particles are not lost to water and wind erosion.
Trench spacing follows the slope, its size suits local climate and soil, it must hold all the water, and its upslope side is protected with grass, shrubs or fabric.
It is one of the techniques used to reverse desertification.

definition.text: Any physical, chemical, mechanical or biological method, alone or combined, of altering a natural soil to meet an engineering purpose.

facts.text: It raises the bearing capacity, tensile strength and overall performance of unstable subsoils, sands and waste materials, chiefly to strengthen roads.
Traditional binders for a road base are bitumen, tar emulsions, asphalt, cement and lime, along with fly ash, cement kiln dust and tree resins.
Bitumen is not environmentally friendly and turns brittle when dry, and Portland cement is often expensive.
Newer stabilizers include enzymes, surfactants, synthetic and bio-polymers, fibre reinforcement and chloride salts; some make hydrophobic layers that keep out water and frost.
Many so-called green products work like soap powder, only lubricating and realigning soil without binding it, while many new approaches rely on clay's binding properties.
The Deep Mixing Method injects through a small probe to strengthen weak or loose soil strata and repair sinkholes.
Adding materials to stabilize a soil can also limit its ability to shrink and swell.

definition.text: Strengthening a soil layer by confining the movement of its particles, for example with geogrids or three-dimensional geocells.

facts.text: Geogrids confine aggregate by interlocking with it, while geocells confine it by the hoop stress of their cell walls.
On Swedish forest roads, geocell-reinforced sections markedly raised bearing capacity and reduced permanent deformation under repeated traffic.
Locally sourced infill in geocells may perform as well as or better than imported crushed aggregate.
Better drainage, for instance with stone mattresses, also stabilizes roads by removing excess pore water and spreading loads.

title: Magnesium chloride dust control

definition.text: Spreading magnesium chloride on unpaved roads and dusty sites, where its moisture-absorbing nature keeps fine particles from becoming airborne.

facts.text: It absorbs water from air at 32% relative humidity, keeping the surface damp and binding gravel and clay particles to the road.
It works better in humid than in arid climates, and its chief benefit is lower maintenance costs for gravel roads.
Its use is controversial: advocates cite cleaner air and safer roads, but the dissolved salts reach groundwater and surface water, where chloride above 250 mg/L is regulated.
Salts accumulating in roadside soils harm plants by raising the osmotic pressure of the soil solution, altering mineral nutrition and building toxic ion levels.

contested_note: The source calls road use of magnesium chloride controversial, weighing dust and safety benefits against chloride pollution of water, soil and plants.

title: Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936
article: Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936

definition.text: A US federal law of 1936 that let the government pay farmers to cut production in order to conserve soil and prevent erosion.

facts.text: It was passed after the Supreme Court declared the Agricultural Adjustment Act unconstitutional.
It amended and renamed the Soil Conservation Act of 1935 to preserve soil fertility and reduce exploitation and unprofitable use of national soil resources.
Landlords now had to share the government payments with the sharecroppers and tenants who worked their land.
It directed soil conservation on the Dust Bowl's high plains, educating farmers and planting trees and native grass.

sources.title: Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936

title: Great Plains Shelterbelt

definition.text: A US project, begun in 1934, to plant windbreaks across the Great Plains states.

facts.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt started it in response to the Dust Bowl's dust storms; the Forest Service expected trees around farms to cut wind speed and evaporation of soil moisture.
By 1942, 30,233 shelterbelts held 220 million trees over 18,600 square miles (48,000 km2), in a 100-mile wide zone from North Dakota's Canadian border to the Brazos River in Texas.
Farmers were paid to plant and tend native trees such as red cedar and green ash along fence rows; the first tree, an Austrian pine, went into an Oklahoma farm in 1935.
Because a long-term project was ineligible for emergency relief funds, Roosevelt moved it to the Works Progress Administration, helped by the Forest Service and Civilian Conservation Corps.
By 2010 many of the shelterbelts were old and declining, and federal grants funded their renovation in Kansas, North Dakota, South Dakota and Nebraska.

notes: Dust Bowl (S:17f77c4fbcc2) describes the belt as more than 200 million trees running to Abilene, Texas; consistent with the 220 million count, but the southern end differs from the Brazos River. S:03ff06eb038f is flagged CONTESTED for a funding dispute, not a disagreement between sources.

definition.text: An earth terrace on a hillside, typical of the ancient field systems of the British Isles.

facts.text: Lynchets often run in vertical rows, called strip lynchets, mostly in southern Britain near Iron Age forts and older earthworks.
The traditional theory is that long ploughing makes soil slip downslope, building a positive lynchet where the surface rises and a negative lynchet where it drops.
The size, spacing and number of rows show that many were man-made, most likely dug to make the most of land for farming.
The word is the diminutive of lynch, an old term for an agricultural terrace.

definition.text: A land use system that integrates trees with crops or pasture.

facts.text: It is managed to optimize interactions among the plants and animals, using the forest as a model, which makes it applied agroecology.
The term was coined in 1973 by forester John Bene, though the practices are millennia old.
In 2025, 91 countries and areas reported 55.4 million hectares under agroforestry, most of it in Asia.
Groundcover protects depleted soil from erosion, and trees slow runoff and evaporation so more water infiltrates.
Nitrogen-fixing plants such as legumes can restore soil nitrogen fertility.
It can increase carbon stocks in soil and woody biomass.
The USDA lists five temperate practices: alley cropping, forest farming, riparian forest buffers, silvopasture and windbreaks.
Honduras's Quesungual system replaced slash-and-burn hillside farming, whose exposed soil washed away, by keeping nitrogen-fixing trees that cut erosion and hold moisture.

definition.text: A small, sometimes temporary dam built across a swale, ditch or waterway to counter erosion by slowing the water.

facts.text: It flattens the channel gradient, slowing the flow, which induces infiltration and reduces erosion; it is not mainly a sediment trap.
Coarse and medium sediment settles behind it while finer grains pass through.
In arid areas check dams are built to increase groundwater recharge.
They are made of rocks, gravel, logs, hay bales or sandbags and are usually less than 2 to 3 feet high.

definition.text: Strips of native perennial vegetation placed within row-crop fields to protect soil and water and support biodiversity.

facts.text: Setting aside 10% of a corn field can reduce sediment movement by 95%, and cut runoff losses of phosphorus and nitrogen by 90% and 85%.
Native prairie plants stabilize soil and concentrate more organic carbon in it than corn and soybean.
They are placed as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters, often on hard-to-farm areas.
They supported twice as many aphid-eating insects as soybean fields.

definition.text: Removing sediment and contaminants from stormwater runoff by passing it through planted soil, where plants and microbes hold and break down pollutants.

facts.text: A bioretention area typically has a sand bed, a layered filter-media soil and plants on top; stored water seeps into the underlying soils over a period of days.
Pollutants are treated by filtration, adsorption, chemical transformation and biological degradation; clay in the planting soil supplies adsorption sites for hydrocarbons, heavy metals and nutrients.
Loamy sand sites suit it best, since the dug soil can be reused; clay content above 25 percent or slopes above 20 percent may rule it out.
In laboratory tests cells removed 94%, 88%, 95% and over 95% of zinc, copper, lead and cadmium, but their capacity is finite, so the media eventually needs replacing.

definition.text: A strip of land kept under permanent vegetation, mostly on farmland, to protect soil, water and air quality.

facts.text: By slowing surface runoff, buffer strips trap sediment and filter out nutrients and pesticides before they reach surface waters.
Roots of the planted vegetation bind soil particles, reducing wind erosion and stabilizing stream banks against erosion and landslides.
Vegetation ranges from grass alone to mixes of grass, trees and shrubs; more diverse strips give more protection from nutrient and pesticide flow.
Governments often pay for buffer strips because they cut nitrogen losses to water and soil loss by wind erosion.
Soil drainage is the first criterion for siting grasses: poor drainage causes ponding, high drainage is droughty, and medium drainage suits planting best.
The NRCS finds contour strip cropping most effective on slopes of 4 to 8%.

definition.text: Strips of perennial vegetation alternating with wider cultivated strips of cropland across a slope.

facts.text: They work best when runoff arrives evenly as sheet flow, and are well suited to trapping pesticides and reducing rill erosion.
They need to be at least 15 feet (4.6 m) wide and can often serve as a cheap substitute for terraces.
Vegetative barriers are a narrower version: rows of hardy native perennial grasses or shrubs that reduce wind and water erosion and trap sediment.

definition.text: A band of grass or other permanent vegetation at a field's edge that shields riparian areas from sediment, pesticides, pathogens and nutrients in runoff.

facts.text: Filter strips matter for protecting stream banks and water quality, and work best when other practices steer water toward them.
Once mainly agricultural, they are now common in urban areas where water quality is a growing concern.
Field borders, strips of perennial vegetation on cropland edges, reduce wind and water erosion but only help with runoff that flows across them.

definition.text: A soil and water conservation system built on hedgerows of the vetiver grass.

facts.text: Planted across a slope, vetiver forms a dense barrier that slows and spreads runoff; sediment built up behind the hedge gradually forms a lasting terrace.
Its roots can reach 3–4 m deep in the first year, and it tolerates roughly pH 3 to pH 11 and most heavy metals.
A good hedge can cut rainfall runoff by as much as 70% and sediment by as much as 90%.
It is used in more than 100 countries, for erosion and sediment control, slope stabilization and phytoremediation.
